column1: # Three tab-separated columns, no header row:
# `scheme` names a romanisation convention. Every row of a scheme is applied
# together, so a name produces one Latin spelling per scheme and the builder
# indexes each of them beside the Cyrillic name.
#   national    the official Ukrainian transliteration (Cabinet of Ministers
#               resolution 55, 2010). It is what passports, road signs and
#               Ukrainian `name:en` mostly follow, so it is the one a reader
#               who has seen the name written officially will type.
#   pragmatic   how people actually type Ukrainian in a Latin keyboard: г as
#               g (not h), и as i (not y), х as h (not kh), ц as c (not ts),
#               щ as sch (not shch). It is not a standard. It exists because a
#               search box is not a passport office.
# `position` is `any` or `start`. The 2010 rules spell є, ї, й, ю and я
# differently at the start of a word (ye, yi, y, yu, ya) and inside it (ie, i,
# i, iu, ia); every other row is `any`.
# `source` is a run of Cyrillic letters, folded before it is matched: lower
# case, no apostrophes. A multi-letter source wins over its first letter, which
# is how the official "зг -> zgh" rule keeps Згода distinct from Жода. Russian
# letters are present because Ukrainian OSM data carries Russian names
# (`name:ru`), and they romanise rather than pass through.
# `target` is Latin. An empty target drops the letter (ь, ъ). The table is
# compiled into the reader with `include_str!`, applied at build time only, and
# validated by `transliteration::tests`: an unknown scheme, a duplicate row, a
# Cyrillic target or an empty source fails the build's tests.
# To add a spelling, add a row. It reaches existing names when the section is
# rebuilt; nothing about it is read on the query side.
